title: A Little Leaven: Discipline in a Proud Church
summary: Paul confronts a case of incest the Corinthian church has tolerated: a man is living with his father's wife. He tells them to remove the man from their fellowship, using the Passover image of clearing out old leaven, and corrects a misunderstanding of his earlier letter: believers are not to withdraw from sinners in the world, but they must not share fellowship with a professing believer who persists in open sin.
story: The first four chapters of the letter dealt with the church's quarrels over leaders and its infatuation with worldly wisdom. Now Paul turns to reports of moral failure, beginning with the most shocking one. The link with what came before is pride: the same church that boasted of its wisdom was “proud” while tolerating a sin that outsiders would have condemned (verse 2). This chapter opens a section (chapters 5 and 6) on sexual morality and on how the church relates to the world, and it prepares for the longer discussion of marriage in chapter 7. It also shows something that runs through the whole letter: Paul treats the church as a single body whose health every member affects.
historical:
First Corinthians was written from Ephesus (16:8), probably around AD 53 to 55, a few years after Paul had founded the church during a stay of about eighteen months (Acts 18:11). Paul had heard news of the church from members of Chloe's household (1:11), and a delegation of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus had arrived (16:17), probably carrying a letter with the church's questions (7:1). This chapter responds to something “actually reported” (verse 1), not to one of their written questions.

Verse 9 mentions an earlier letter Paul had written to them, telling them not to associate with sexually immoral people. That letter has not survived. The Corinthians apparently took it to mean withdrawing from all immoral people in the city, an impossibility in a Roman commercial center, and Paul clarifies what he meant. Some interpreters wonder whether the man disciplined here is the offender Paul later asks the church to forgive in 2 Corinthians 2:5-11; many modern scholars think that person was someone who had wronged Paul himself, so the identification is uncertain.
cultural:
“A man has his father's wife” (verse 1) almost certainly describes a man living with his stepmother, either after his father's death or divorce, since Paul does not call her the man's mother. The law of Moses forbade such a union (Leviticus 18:8), and so did Roman law and custom, which is why Paul says it was intolerable “even among pagans.” The woman is not addressed, which suggests she was not a member of the church. Why the church tolerated it is unclear. Some suggest the man was a wealthy patron whom few would challenge; others think some members took their new spiritual freedom to mean that bodily conduct no longer mattered, a view Paul answers in chapter 6.

The leaven imagery comes from Passover. Before the feast, Jewish households searched their homes and removed every trace of leaven (Exodus 12:15-20), and for seven days they ate unleavened bread. Leaven was a bit of old fermented dough kept back to raise a new batch, and a small amount spread through the whole lump. The closing command, “Expel the wicked man from among you” (verse 13), echoes a formula repeated in Deuteronomy for removing evil from Israel's community (for example Deuteronomy 17:7). Eating together, mentioned in verse 11, was a sign of fellowship and acceptance in the ancient world, and for Christians it included the shared meal at which they celebrated the Lord's Supper.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 to 5 state the case and give a verdict, with Paul present “in spirit” at a formal church assembly. Verses 6 to 8 build an extended metaphor from Passover: leaven, dough, lamb, and feast. Verses 9 to 13 correct the misreading of the earlier letter and draw a line between those “outside” and those “inside” the church. Rhetorical questions carry the argument (“Do you not know...?” appears here for the first of many times in the letter), and the chapter ends with a quotation from Deuteronomy that turns Israel's covenant discipline into the church's.

outline.t: Incest tolerated and a church puffed up
Paul's judgment: hand the man over to Satan
Clean out the old leaven: Christ our Passover
The earlier letter clarified: not the world, but the professing brother
Judging insiders, leaving outsiders to God

doctrines.note: The church is a holy community whose life together matters. Discipline is exercised by the gathered assembly in the name of the Lord Jesus, not by one leader acting alone, and it concerns those who claim to belong, not the surrounding world.

Paul tells the church to become what it already is: “a new unleavened batch, as you really are” (verse 7). Holiness is first God's gift in Christ and then a calling to live out, which is why tolerated sin contradicts the church's identity.

“Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (verse 7) is one of the New Testament's clearest links between the death of Jesus and the Passover. As the lamb's blood marked Israel's rescue from Egypt, Christ's death marks the start of a new exodus and a new people.

words.note: Zume, leaven or yeast. In the ancient world this was a piece of old fermented dough, not packaged yeast, and a little of it spread through a whole batch. Jesus used it both positively (the kingdom grows like leaven) and negatively (the leaven of the Pharisees). Here it pictures how tolerated sin and pride spread through a community.

Pascha, Passover, and here the Passover lamb. The word came into Greek from Aramaic. Paul's phrase ties Jesus's death, which took place at Passover in all four Gospels, to the lamb whose blood protected Israel in Exodus 12, and turns the whole Christian life into a festival kept with sincerity and truth.

Paradidomi, to hand over or deliver. The same verb is used for Judas handing Jesus over and for passing on a tradition (11:23; 15:3). Here the church is to “hand this man over to Satan” (verse 5), meaning at least putting him outside the community's protection and fellowship, with the stated goal that he be saved.

Phusioo, to puff up or inflate. It is a favorite word of this letter (used six times in 1 Corinthians and only once elsewhere in the New Testament). Paul diagnoses the church's problem as swollen self-importance: they were proud of their tolerance when they should have grieved.

christ: The chapter's theological center is one sentence: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (verse 7). Paul assumes the Corinthians, most of them Gentiles, understand that Jesus died at Passover and that his death fulfills what the Passover lamb pictured, rescue from judgment and the birth of a free people. The church's holiness rests on that finished sacrifice, not on its own achievement. Even discipline is aimed at salvation: the goal of removing the man is that “his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord” (verse 5). Christ's death both makes the church a new batch and gives hope to the one who has been put out.

hard.q: What does it mean to “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh”?
hard.a:
The phrase is difficult, and interpreters read it in two main ways. Many take it as excommunication: putting the man out of the church, the sphere where Christ reigns, back into the world, which Paul regards as Satan's domain. On this reading “flesh” means the sinful nature (as it often does in Paul), and the hope is that exclusion will bring him to repentance so that his spirit is saved. Others take “flesh” more physically and think Paul expected bodily suffering or illness to follow, comparing 11:30, where some Corinthians became sick through abusing the Lord's Supper. Either way, the purpose clause matters: the aim is restoration, not destruction of the person.

A related question is whether church discipline is harsh or loving. Paul's own answer is that ignoring the sin was the unloving choice, both for the man and for the church, and that the goal is his salvation. He also limits discipline to professing believers: those outside are left to God's judgment (verses 12 and 13), and Christians are not to withdraw from the world.

questions: Paul says the Corinthians were proud when they should have grieved. Why might a community take pride in tolerating something that is harming one of its members?
Paul tells the church not to cut itself off from sinners in the world but to hold its own members to account. Why do churches so often reverse those two?
What would it look like for discipline in a church to aim, as Paul does, at the restoration of the person being disciplined?
